title: Cleaning a river
hook: volunteers cleaned the Kali Bein, the river where Nanak disappeared, by kar seva

segments.voice: Yesterday, tasveer, and your line was a painting, not a photo. Today, something old comes back to life, and this time it's a river. Day one thousand forty-one.

Mud up to the knees. A line of volunteers stands in a narrow, choked stream, passing buckets of black silt and tangled weeds from hand to hand up the bank. Some are farmers. Some are students. Some came after work. Nobody is paid. The water barely moves, and it smells. But the stories of Guru Nanak know the name of this stream. It's the Kali Bein, at Sultanpur Lodhi, the river where, the stories say, Nanak went into the water and vanished. Today, cleaning a river.
screen: `MUD TO THE KNEES.` → `BUCKETS UP THE BANK.` → `THE KALI BEIN.`

segments.voice: First, the river in the story. The janamsakhis, the old stories of Guru Nanak, tell of the morning he went to bathe in the Bein and vanished. Tradition says he was gone for three days, and that when he came back, his first words were: there is no Hindu, there is no Muslim. This path told that story long ago. Today, the river itself. Second, what happened to the river. In our own times the Kali Bein was choked with weeds and waste, and dirty water ran into it. The river of that story was hard to recognize. Third, the hands. Volunteers began to clean it by kar seva, the Sikh name for free, hands-on work for a sacred place, the same kind of work that has cleaned the pools at gurdwaras. A Sikh sant, Balbir Singh Seechewal, is known for leading it. They cleared weeds and silt by hand, worked on stopping the dirty water, and planted the banks. Over time, the water ran again. Fourth, the root. In the Asa di Var, at Ang 472, Guru Nanak says that first of all, water is life, by which everything is made green. If water is where life begins, then a dirty river isn't only an eyesore. It's a wound in the place the Guru called life itself. So the volunteers didn't treat it as a project. They treated it as seva. That's today's line: clean the river. The Guru disappeared into that water. They made sure there was water worth coming back out of.
screen: `NANAK VANISHED INTO THE BEIN.` · `THE RIVER CHOKED WITH WASTE.` · `KAR SEVA, BUCKET BY BUCKET.` · `FIRST, WATER IS LIFE.` · then, large: `CLEAN THE RIVER.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with water. Sit, and if you can, set a glass of water in front of you. Look at it. Breathe in, and think of where it came from: a river, a reservoir, rain on a hillside far away. Breathe out, and think of where it goes when you're done with it. Somewhere downstream, someone else drinks it, or a field, or a fish. Let the breath be slow and plain. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. Then take one sip, and notice it. The bell holds the time.
Kali Bein. The river at Sultanpur Lodhi where tradition says Guru Nanak disappeared and came back with his first teaching, cleared by volunteers through kar seva. Today's word.

Your line: clean the river. Today, pick up litter near water: a creek, a drain, a beach, a fountain, even a gutter that runs to a stream. Do it safely, with gloves or a bag. Day one thousand forty-one.

howItsDone: Kar seva is volunteer labor for a sacred place, such as cleaning a gurdwara's sarovar or building and repairing gurdwaras. At Sultanpur Lodhi, volunteers have cleaned the Kali Bein by kar seva, and Sikhs visit the Gurdwara Ber Sahib there, linked with the story of Guru Nanak's disappearance in the river.
